claims.text: A controlled heat treatment can induce nanoscale phase segregation or coherent precipitate formation in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Magnetic high-entropy alloys in typical as-cast or homogenized states have largely disordered microstructures.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates act as effective domain-wall-pinning sites.
Finely distributed coherent precipitates impede domain-wall motion in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases the energy required for magnetic-domain reversal.
The increased reversal energy caused by precipitate pinning raises the coercive field.
Heat-treatment-induced nanoscale segregation will measurably increase coercive field relative to a homogenized alloy without that segregation.
Annealing temperature can alter the length scale and phase state of decomposition in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The coercivity increase should hold under room-temperature magnetic characterization.
The beneficial effect requires precipitates to remain nanoscale and coherent with the matrix.
Precipitate overgrowth or coarsening may negate the pinning effect and may decrease coercivity.
Excessive secondary-phase formation may negate the pinning effect and may decrease coercivity.
The magnitude of coercivity enhancement may depend on heat-treatment conditions and alloy composition.
Coercive field can be obtained from magnetic hysteresis loops measured by vibrating-sample magnetometry or a similar method.
TEM and SEM analysis will verify precipitate presence, size, distribution, and coherence.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to form nanoscale coherent precipitates would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies a standard homogenized state as the comparator, whereas the baseline permits either an as-cast or homogenized state; these are not necessarily equivalent matched baselines.

The boundary says the coercivity prediction applies only when nanoscale coherent precipitates form, but the falsification rule treats failure to form those precipitates as falsification rather than failure to realize the intervention's required mediator.
